newsitem.title: FRANCE: Juppe departures clears way for Chirac appeal.
newsitem.headline: Juppe departures clears way for Chirac appeal.

text.p: French Prime Minister Alain Juppe's decision to fall on his sword after the left-wing opposition's success in the first round of a parliamentary election gives President Jacques Chirac a chance to save his presidency.
But it could be an even more risky gamble than Chirac's initial decision to dissolve parliament and call a snap poll 10 months ahead of schedule, analysts said.

Voters dealt France's "ruling couple" a stunning setback in Sunday's ballot, giving the combined left-wing opposition a four-point lead over the centre-right in what was widely seen as a protest against austerity, high taxes and record unemployment.
The mainstream conservatives polled their lowest score since the Fifth Republic was founded in 1958, with the extreme-right National Front winning a record 15 percent.
Juppe took responsibility on Monday, saying he had decided to resign whatever the outcome of next Sunday's decisive runoff.
"We need a new team led by a new prime minister," he said.

Given Juppe's wide unpopularity, conservative politicians are looking anxiously to Chirac to intervene before the second round in a bid to save himself from becoming the prisoner of a hostile, left-wing government.
An official source said the president was expected to address the nation soon but would not express a preference for a successor to the outgoing prime minister.
"That is a very risky move. At least with Juppe, people knew who they were voting for. Now they are going to be asked to vote without knowing for whom," a European diplomat said.
A government source acknowledged that it would be difficult for the centre-right to convey a coherent policy line without a clear standard-bearer.

While Chirac can say he has heeded the voters' message, it is not clear what arguments he can find to sway an electorate which punished him for failing to keep his 1995 presidential campaign promises to bring down unemployment and cut taxes.

"Chirac should never be underestimated in this kind of situation. He thrives on difficulty and comebacks. But the coalition no longer has a captain, a credible discourse or a platform," said Serge July, publisher of the Liberation daily.
If the president vows to make a fresh start with new faces, he will need to indicate what new policies they might pursue.
Yet each of the alternatives embodied by the most prominent candidates for the premiership contain risks.

Popular, socially minded Gaullist Philippe Seguin might win back working-class votes from the extreme-right, but his Euroscepticism and support for strong state control frightens some in the financial markets.
Economic liberals such as ex-prime minister Edouard Balladur or former finance minister Alain Madelin are popular with business but alienate voters seeking a strong, protective state.
Chirac's attempt to make a pitch for the pro-European middle-ground of French politics last week by stressing the need for France to speak with one voice in Europe was a flop.
The first-round vote showed many voters were hostile to or anxious about conditions for joining a single European currency.

One idea Chirac might revive is promising voters another say at a future date on European integration through a referendum. He raised that proposal at the outset of his presidential campaign in 1994 only to drop it after critics objected that France had already voted to approve a single European currency.
The president's other first-round intervention was to assail the Socialists' record and proposals. It too backfired.

Some analysts say that since the coalition needs to win over electors who voted for the extreme-right National Front on the first round, it should run a law-and-order, anti-immigration campaign for the second round.

Chirac could give a more prominent role to hardline Interior Minister Jean-Louis Debre and his Gaullist predecessor, Charles Pasqua, author of a controversial law restricting the conditions for acquiring French citizenship.
But that could alienate centrist voters and might not be credible with supporters of hard-right leader Jean-Marie Le Pen, who often jokes that "the French people prefer the original to the copy".
Chirac's ultimate "nuclear" weapon would be to threaten to resign himself if voters disavow him, as his political mentor, president Charles de Gaulle, did in 1969.
The risk would then be that voters took him at his word, as they did with De Gaulle.
